33 A lightning strike transfers 1  1020 electrons past a point in a time of 30 s.
What is the average current during the lightning strike?
A
0.5 mA
B
0.5 A
C
500 A
D
500 kA

hints: Notice the question gives a number of electrons $1 \times 10^{20}$, not a charge in coulombs, and a very short time of $30 \, \mu\text{s} = 30 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{s}$.
Connect charge to electron number with $Q = Ne$ using $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C}$, then use average current $I = Q/t$.
Check your powers of 10 carefully: the numerator is about $16 \, \text{C}$ and the denominator is $10^{-5} \, \text{s}$, so expect a current of order $10^{5} \, \text{A}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: number of electrons $N = 1 \times 10^{20}$ passing a point in time $t = 30 \, \mu\text{s} = 30 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{s}$.
State the governing physics: total charge is $Q = Ne$ where elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C}$, and average current is $I = Q/t$.
Compare with the options: this is closest to $500 \, \text{kA}$. This is option D.

A.explanation: Far too small because it ignores the huge charge of $1 \times 10^{20}$ electrons and the very short $30 \, \mu\text{s}$ time.

B.explanation: Far too small and results from errors with powers of 10 when converting $30 \, \mu\text{s}$ and using the electron charge.

C.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 1000, often from treating $30 \, \mu\text{s}$ as $30 \, \text{ms}$.

D.explanation: Matches $I = Ne/t$ with $N = 1 \times 10^{20}$ and $t = 30 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{s}$, giving about $5 \times 10^{5} \, \text{A}$.
